title: Vinyl/DVS Scratch Setup & Slipmats
skill: Set up turntables or DVS with the right slipmats and tonearm settings for responsive scratching.
content:
The scratch chain

A scratch setup is a feedback loop between your hand and your ear: hand moves the record, stylus reads it, mixer routes it, and you react. Every component is tuned to make that loop fast and forgiving. Whether you scratch real vinyl or use DVS (Digital Vinyl System) with timecode control records, the physical setup is nearly identical. The deck must be a direct-drive turntable with high torque — belt-drive decks stall when you stop the platter and are useless for scratching. The Technics SL-1200 series and clones like the Pioneer PLX-1000 or Reloop RP-8000 are the standard because of their torque and tank-like build.

Tonearm and cartridge settings

The needle skipping out of the groove under hard hand movement is the single most common beginner problem. You fix it with tracking force, anti-skate, and cartridge choice.

SettingMusic/mixingScratchingWhy
Tracking force2.0-2.5 g3.0-4.0 g (to cart max)Heavier weight keeps the stylus pinned in the groove during fast reversals
Anti-skateMatch force0Anti-skate pulls the arm and causes skips during back-cuts
Cartridge typeEllipticalSpherical/conicalConical tips ride heavier grooves and resist jumping
Height (VTA)LevelSlightly raised at backHelps the tip dig in on worn battle records

Classic scratch cartridges are the Shure M44-7, Ortofon Concorde Scratch/Digi, and Audio-Technica AT-XP series. Concorde-style integrated cartridges screw straight onto the headshell and are the easiest to set up. Set the counterweight by zeroing the arm to balance, then dialing the front ring to your target grams.

Slipmats

The slipmat lets the record slip freely while the platter keeps spinning underneath. For scratching you want a slippery, low-friction mat so the record moves the instant your hand moves it and there is no drag. Many scratch DJs run a slick mat (felt that has been broken in, or a dedicated slick like the Dr. Suzuki Mix Edition) and add a slip sheet — a thin sheet of wax paper, vinyl, or a butter rug — between the mat and the record to kill friction further. Some put a 7-inch piece of vinyl or a beer mat under the center for extra glide.

Felt side down, slick up. If your record drags or 'snaps back' slowly, add a slip sheet under it. If the platter feels like it is fighting your hand, your mat has too much grip — break it in or replace it.

DVS specifics

With Serato, Rekordbox DVS, Traktor Scratch, or VirtualDJ you feed the turntable output into a phono input on a DVS-enabled mixer or audio interface, and the software reads the timecode signal. Set the deck to Absolute (ABS) mode for scratching so the needle position maps directly to the track. Watch the signal scope in software: you want a clean round ring at near-100% quality. A weak or oval scope means dirty needles, low tracking force, or grounding hum. Use fresh, clean timecode records — worn control vinyl is the number-one cause of skipping and drift in DVS scratching.

Mixer and final checks

Set channel gain so the loudest part of your scratch sample peaks just below clipping. Confirm the crossfader is set to a sharp/fast cut curve (more on that next lesson) and that fader reverse is off until you want it. Ground the turntable to the mixer to kill the 60-cycle hum. Now move the record by hand with the fader open and listen: clean sound, no skip, instant response. That is a scratch-ready station.
exercise: Set up one deck for scratching. Set tracking force to about 3.5 g, anti-skate to 0, drop a slick slipmat with a slip sheet under your record, and confirm in DVS (or by ear on vinyl) that you can rub the record fast with zero skip. Adjust force up in 0.25 g steps until skipping stops.

title: The Baby Scratch & Record Control
skill: Perform a clean baby scratch and control the record's movement with both hands.
content:
The foundation scratch

The baby scratch is the simplest scratch and the one every other technique is built from. It is just the sample pushed forward and pulled back with the crossfader fully open the whole time — no fader cuts. Master clean record control here and the named scratches become combinations of this motion with fader work. The sound you scratch with is almost always a short vocal sample, the classic being the 'aaah' or 'fresh' from a battle record. Cue it at the very start of that sound (we cover finding it precisely in lesson 4).

Hand position

Place your scratch hand flat on the record with your fingertips, not your palm — fingers give control, the palm gives drag. The contact point is usually around the label edge or just into the grooves near where the sound sits. Your forearm should be relaxed; the motion comes from the wrist and forearm, not a stiff push from the shoulder. Keep your other hand on or near the crossfader at all times, even when it is doing nothing, so it is always ready.

Both hands always work. Beginners freeze the fader hand. Train both hands to live on the equipment from day one — the fader hand resting on the fader, the record hand on the wax — so transitions between scratches are instant.

The motion

  1. Forward push: from the cue point, push the record forward so the sample plays forward. Push only as far as the sound lasts — for a short 'ah', that is a small move.
  2. Pull back: drag the record backward to return it to the cue point. The sample now plays in reverse.
  3. Repeat rhythmically: forward-back, forward-back. The crossfader stays fully open the entire time, so you hear both the forward and the backward sound.

That forward-and-reverse pair is one baby scratch. Speed it up and you get the recognizable 'wakka-wakka' rub.

Timing it to a beat

Scratching is rhythm, not noise. Put on a beat (or use the metronome/beat on the other deck) at around 90-95 BPM and place your scratches on the beat. Start by doing one forward-back per beat — a quarter-note baby scratch. Then try two per beat (eighth notes). Counting out loud, 'one-and, two-and,' keeps your hand honest. The goal is even, repeatable spacing, not speed.

Common faultCauseFix
Sound drifts off-cuePull-back travels farther than pushMake the back stroke exactly equal the forward stroke
Muddy, smeared soundMoving too slow / too farShorten the stroke to just the sample length
Rushed and unevenTension in forearmRelax wrist; count out loud to a slow beat
SkipsSetup issue, not techniqueRecheck tracking force/anti-skate from lesson 1

Record control drills

Beyond the baby scratch, train pure control: hold the record perfectly still against the spinning platter (the 'pause'), then release. Practice marking a single spot on the label with a sticker and returning to it exactly after every stroke. Practice slow, deliberate forward-only drags and reverse-only drags so each direction sounds clean on its own. This isolation is what lets you later add precise fader cuts to one direction without the other leaking through.

Spend real time here. A scratch DJ with a flawless baby scratch and dead-accurate cue return will out-perform someone who rushed to flares with sloppy fundamentals. Aim for five minutes of metronome-locked baby scratches before every practice session for the rest of your scratching life.
exercise: Lock a baby scratch to a beat. Put a sticker on the record at your cue, run a 90 BPM beat, and do one even forward-back baby scratch per beat for two minutes, keeping the sticker returning to the same spot. Then double up to two per beat without losing the cue.

title: Core Scratches: Forward, Chirp, Scribble, Transformer, Flare
skill: Execute forward, chirp, scribble, transformer and intro flare scratches cleanly and in time.
content:
From baby scratch to named techniques

Every named scratch is the baby-scratch hand motion plus a specific crossfader pattern. The fader decides which parts of the forward and backward strokes the audience hears. Set your crossfader to a sharp cut curve so a tiny movement fully opens or closes the channel. We will build five core scratches in order of difficulty.

1. Forward scratch

Push the record forward (sound plays forward), then close the fader and pull the record back in silence. The listener hears only forward stabs. It is a baby scratch with the backward half muted. Practice clean, even forward stabs on the beat — this teaches you to cut the fader closed the instant your forward push ends.

2. Chirp

The chirp gets its bird-like sound by cutting both ends. Start with the fader open and the record still. Push forward and as you reach the end of the push, close the fader; then open the fader at the very start of the pull-back and close again as the back stroke ends. The result is a short forward 'chi' and a short backward 'rp'. The trick is synchronizing the fader close with the moment the record changes direction. It is the first scratch where your two hands must hit a precise simultaneous mark.

3. Scribble

The scribble is a fast, tense baby scratch with the fader open — no fader work at all. You tense your forearm and vibrate the record back and forth in very short, rapid strokes, like a fast tremble. It builds the forearm tension and speed you need for transformers and flares. Keep strokes tiny and fast; the sound is a buzzing 'rrrrr'.

4. Transformer

Here the record moves slowly and steadily in one direction while the fader chops the sound on and off rapidly. You 'click' the fader open and shut repeatedly (tapping it open from a closed rest position, or stabbing it shut from open) as the sample plays through. The effect is a stuttering, robotic chopping of a held note. Practice tapping the fader in even subdivisions — two, three, four taps per record stroke.

5. Flare (intro)

The flare is built around clicks: a click is one quick close-and-open of the fader in the middle of a stroke. A one-click flare means the fader starts open, you interrupt the stroke with a single momentary close, then it stays open. So a forward stroke becomes 'sound — click — sound', giving two bursts from one push. Because the fader rests open, you can chain flares much faster than chirps. Start with the one-click flare in both directions before attempting two-click (the orbit).

ScratchFader at restFader actionRecord motion
ForwardOpenClose on the pull-backPush forward, pull back silent
ChirpOpenClose at each direction changeShort forward + short back
ScribbleOpenNoneFast tense vibration
TransformerClosedTap open repeatedlySlow steady drag
FlareOpenMomentary click(s) mid-strokeNormal forward/back
Slow before fast. Practice every fader pattern at half speed against a slow beat until it is perfectly clean. Speed is a by-product of accuracy — never the goal itself. A clean slow flare beats a sloppy fast one in any battle.

Putting them in time

Run a beat around 90 BPM and assign one scratch per bar: bar one forward, bar two chirp, bar three scribble, bar four transformer. This forces you to switch techniques in rhythm and is the seed of a routine. Record yourself and check that each scratch lands on the beat and that the cue sound returns to the same spot every time.
exercise: Drill the five core scratches to a slow beat. At 90 BPM, do four bars each of forward, chirp, scribble, and transformer scratches, then attempt eight bars of one-click flares. Keep the fader on a sharp cut curve and return to your cue exactly each cycle.

title: Clock Theory & Cueing the Sound
skill: Find and cue the right sound on the record using clock theory to start any scratch precisely.
content:
Why you need a system to find the sound

Every scratch starts at a precise point in the groove — the exact frame where your chosen sample begins. If you cue half a millimeter early you get silence before the stab; half a millimeter late and you clip the front of the sound. Clock theory is the turntablist's mental map for finding and returning to that point instantly, even mid-routine, without looking.

The record as a clock face

Imagine the platter as a clock. The point nearest you (6 o'clock, where the record meets your body) and the top (12 o'clock) are your anchors. You reference the position of the marker dot you place on the record relative to those clock positions. When the sample's start sits at 6 o'clock under the needle, you know your hand is at the cue. After a scratch, you return the record so the marker is back at the same clock position, and the sound is re-cued perfectly.

Mark your records. Put a bright sticker or a paint-pen dot on the label aligned to where the sample begins under the stylus. Most scratch DJs use the label-edge text as a natural clock reference too. The dot is your visual cue; the clock is your muscle-memory cue.

Finding the sound

  1. Drop the needle roughly where the sample lives and play it forward at normal hand speed to hear the whole sound.
  2. Slowly rock the record back until the sample just stops making sound — that silent edge is the true start of the sample.
  3. Park there. Place your sticker at 6 o'clock (or wherever is comfortable) so that this start point is your zero.
  4. Push forward from zero: the sample should fire instantly with no dead air and no clipped front.

This 'find the silent edge then mark it' process is how you cue any sample — a vocal stab, a kick, a horn hit. The cleaner your cue, the cleaner every scratch built on it.

Clock positions and stroke length

Different sounds need different stroke lengths, and clock theory makes those repeatable. A short 'ah' might travel only from 6 to 7 o'clock; a long 'fresh' might run 6 to 9. By learning the clock distance a sample occupies, you stop overshooting (which drags in the next unwanted sound) and stop undershooting (which clips the word).

Sample lengthApprox clock travelUse for
Very short stab ('ah')6 to 6:30Fast baby scratches, flares, chirps
Medium word ('fresh')6 to 7:30Forward scratches, transformers
Long phrase / held note6 to 9 or moreTears, drags, drawn-out transforms

Cueing under pressure

In a routine you will not have time to hunt. Clock theory lets you re-cue by feel: after a combination drifts, you glance at the sticker, see it sitting at 8 o'clock instead of 6, and pull it back two hours to reset — all in a fraction of a beat. This connects to mixing's jog-nudge cueing: it is the same skill of mapping ear to hand position, applied at scratch resolution. Practice cueing the sound with your eyes closed, returning to zero by forearm memory, then opening your eyes to check the sticker landed at 6. When that is reliable, your cueing will never be the weak link in a routine.
exercise: Mark and cue one sample with clock theory. Find the silent edge at the start of your scratch sample, place a sticker so that point sits at 6 o'clock, then do ten forward scratches returning the sticker to 6 every time. Close your eyes for the last five and check your accuracy.

title: Beat Juggling Fundamentals
skill: Juggle a beat across two decks to rearrange and loop drums live by hand.
content:
What beat juggling is

Beat juggling is manipulating two copies of the same beat (or two breaks) across two decks by hand to create new patterns, loops, and drum fills in real time — without software loops. Where scratching plays with a single sound, juggling plays with rhythm and arrangement. You need two copies of the same record (or the same timecode track on both DVS decks) so the same drum hits exist on both platters.

The setup

Cue the identical break on both decks at the same point — for example, on the downbeat (the first kick). Both records marked with a sticker at that downbeat so you can find it instantly (clock theory directly applies). Your crossfader cuts between the two decks; that is how you switch which copy the audience hears. A sharp cut curve is essential so the switches are seamless.

Identical cues are everything. Both records must be cued to the exact same point in the beat and running at the same pitch. If they drift even slightly, your juggle will stumble. Re-cue with your marker dot constantly.

The fundamental move: the loop juggle

The simplest juggle loops a one- or two-beat segment by alternating decks:

  1. Play deck A from the downbeat. Let it play one beat (one kick or a kick-snare).
  2. As deck A finishes that beat, cut the crossfader to deck B, which is cued to the same downbeat, and let B play that same beat.
  3. While B plays, use your free hand to spin deck A back to its downbeat cue, ready to go again.
  4. Cut back to A, play the beat, spin B back. Repeat.

You are alternately playing and re-cueing, so the same segment loops endlessly by hand. This is the core mechanic — every fancier juggle is a variation of play-cut-rewind across two decks.

Rearranging the pattern

Once looping is solid, change where you cut to rearrange drums. By playing a kick from one deck, cutting to grab a snare from the other deck at a different point, and alternating, you can build a pattern that does not exist on the original record — for example doubling up kicks, inserting an extra snare, or stuttering a hit. This is the same hot-cue re-editing idea from the digital lessons, done physically: you are reordering drum hits live.

ElementRole in a juggleTip
Two same recordsProvide duplicate hits to alternateBuy doubles; mark both labels identically
CrossfaderSelects which deck is heardSharp curve, cut on the beat
Free (rewind) handRe-cues the silent deckSpin back to the sticker every cycle
Matched pitchKeeps both copies in timeSet identical pitch faders, check by ear

Timing and counting

Juggling lives or dies on staying in time. Count the beats out loud — 'one, two, cut, one, two, cut' — so your fader cuts and rewinds land exactly on the beat. Start slow with a simple two-beat loop and keep the tempo steady before adding rearrangement. Record yourself and check that the juggled pattern grooves and that no rewind is audible (the rewind must happen on the muted deck). Use a clean, well-known break so you can hear immediately when a hit lands off the grid.

Beat juggling is physically demanding and takes patience — expect weeks to get a clean two-beat loop solid. But it is one of the most impressive live skills a turntablist has, and it sharpens your sense of rhythm in a way nothing else does.
exercise: Build a two-beat loop juggle. With two copies of the same break cued to the downbeat on both decks, play one beat from deck A, cut to deck B for the same beat while rewinding A, and keep the loop going for 16 bars in time. Count aloud and make sure no rewind is heard.

title: Practice Routines & Battle/Showcase Basics
skill: Build a daily practice routine and structure a short battle or showcase set that shows off your skills.
content:
How turntablists actually improve

Scratching and juggling are athletic, motor-skill disciplines. You improve through short, focused, daily reps far more than through occasional long sessions. A structured practice routine prevents the most common trap: noodling the same flare you already know while never fixing your weak hand. Treat practice like a musician treats scales — warm up, isolate weaknesses, then play musically.

A daily 30-minute routine

BlockTimeFocus
Warm-up5 minBaby scratches and cue-return drills to a slow metronome
Fader isolation5 minTransformer taps and flare clicks, fader hand only, on a held sound
Technique focus10 minOne scratch you are weakest at, slow then up to tempo
Combinations5 minChain two techniques in rhythm (e.g. chirp into flare)
Musical play5 minFreestyle over a beat, recording it
Record every session. Your ears lie in the moment. Phone audio is enough — listening back reveals off-time cuts and clipped cues you cannot feel while playing. Keep a folder and compare month to month.

Building cleanliness and speed

Always practice with a metronome or beat, never in silence. Use a tempo you can play perfectly clean and only raise it when every rep is flawless — typically in 2-5 BPM steps. Isolate your weak hand: most DJs neglect fader control, so spend deliberate time on fader-only drills with the record held still. Alternate days emphasizing scratching and days emphasizing juggling so neither skill stalls.

Structuring a battle or showcase routine

A battle round is short — often 1 to 3 minutes — and judged on originality, technical skill, musicality, and crowd reaction. A showcase set is longer and more about flow and entertainment. Either way, structure beats raw difficulty.

  1. Open strong: lead with a recognizable sample or a confident, clean combo so the crowd locks in immediately. Never open with your hardest trick cold.
  2. Build: layer increasingly technical material — move from forwards and chirps into flares, then a beat-juggle section.
  3. Theme it: use a known acapella, a famous break, or a 'word play' concept (scratching sentences) so there is a hook beyond technique.
  4. Peak: place your most impressive, most-rehearsed combo near the end — your signature move.
  5. Close clean: end on a tight, deliberate phrase, not a fizzle. Land the last hit exactly on the beat.

Rehearse the routine end to end until it is muscle memory; in a battle, nerves will rob you of about 20% of your control, so your practiced ceiling must be well above what you need. Prepare your records in advance with clear marker dots, know your cue points cold, and have a backup plan if a needle skips. Crowd-facing skills from peak-time performance apply directly: command the moment, make eye contact, and sell the routine — judges and crowds reward confidence as much as clean cuts.

The mindset

Progress in turntablism is slow and physical. Set tiny weekly goals (a clean two-click flare, a stable two-beat juggle), track them in your recordings, and accept plateaus as normal. Consistency over months is what separates a scratch DJ from someone who owns a turntable.
exercise: Build and record a 60-second routine. Plan an open-build-peak-close structure using two core scratches plus one short beat-juggle, rehearse it to a 90 BPM beat until clean, then record one full take and critique the timing and cue accuracy on playback.
